position: Chapter author's recommendation (Candeub); the chapter notes disagreement among conservatives on parts of the antitrust agenda.
proposal: The FTC should set up an ESG and DEI collusion task force to investigate firms, particularly in private equity, for using such practices to meet targets, fix prices or reduce output, and Congress should investigate ESG practices as cover for anticompetitive conduct. The chapter also calls refusal of service based on political views by large, regulated, market-power firms a possible unfair trade practice.

status_summary: No FTC task force on ESG or DEI collusion was found, and a Federal Register search for FTC documents mentioning ESG since 2025-01-20 returned none. The FTC has pursued related theories through individual cases. It joined DOJ in a 2025-05-22 statement of interest backing state attorneys general who allege that asset managers used coal holdings to restrain output (Texas v. BlackRock). It obtained consent orders barring advertising agencies from coordinating ad placement on publishers' political or ideological viewpoints: Omnicom and Interpublic (proposed 2025-06-23, finalized in September 2025, with terms that also cover DEI-commitment criteria), then WPP, Publicis and Dentsu (2026-04-15, with eight states) and Havas (2026-06-30), with the court later approving those orders. A separate FTC probe of Media Matters over the same boycott allegations was blocked by a preliminary injunction; after argument on 2026-04-13 the FTC withdrew its investigative demand and the D.C. Circuit dismissed the appeal on 2026-05-04. The actions differ from the chapter in design: no task force, no private equity focus, and they rest on Sherman Act and unfair-methods-of-competition theories.

timeline.event: DOJ's Antitrust Division, joined by the FTC, files a statement of interest in Texas v. BlackRock (E.D. Tex.) supporting state attorneys general who allege that BlackRock, State Street and Vanguard used holdings in competing coal producers to induce lower output, and urging denial of the asset managers' motion to dismiss.

FTC announces a proposed consent order in Omnicom's 13.5 billion dollar acquisition of Interpublic that bars coordinating or steering ad spending away from publishers based on political or ideological viewpoints (vote 2-0-1, Commissioner Meador recused); the Federal Register notice follows on 2025-06-26.

FTC approves the final Omnicom and Interpublic order, which trade press reports broadened the restrictions to cover third-party journalistic-standards ratings and DEI commitments as ad-buying criteria (date from the article's publication, which refers to the previous Friday).

D.C. Circuit, 2-1, declines to lift an August 2025 preliminary injunction that bars the FTC from pursuing its civil investigative demand to Media Matters in the advertising-boycott probe; the district court had found the probe likely retaliatory in violation of the First Amendment, and the panel did not rule on the merits.

Thirteen state attorneys general announce a 29.5 million dollar settlement with Vanguard in the same ESG antitrust suit; claims against BlackRock and State Street continue. The sources do not show the FTC or DOJ as parties to the settlement.

At D.C. Circuit argument in the Media Matters appeal, an FTC lawyer says the agency is negotiating settlements with other targets of its probe into whether advertising and media groups colluded to boycott online platforms.

FTC (vote 1-0-1, Commissioner Meador recused), with eight states, files a complaint in the Northern District of Texas against WPP, Publicis and Dentsu alleging collusion through common brand-safety standards, with proposed orders barring agreements on such standards or ad placement limits based on politically motivated criteria; the FTC page says the court later approved all three orders.
After oral argument, the FTC withdraws its civil investigative demand to Media Matters and the D.C. Circuit dismisses the FTC appeal.

FTC and eight states announce a proposed order with Havas Media Group USA (vote 1-0-1, Commissioner Meador recused), described by the FTC as the last of the six large agencies to face such an order; the FTC page says the Northern District of Texas has since approved and finalized it.

title: Create an FTC task force on ESG and DEI collusion and unfair trade practices
uncertainties: Whether the FTC has an internal ESG or DEI working group that was never announced cannot be ruled out; only the Federal Register (zero FTC documents mentioning ESG) and press coverage were checked. The 2026 WPP, Publicis, Dentsu and Havas events now rest on the FTC's own releases (an earlier attempt at a different FTC URL returned a 404); the dates of the court approvals of those orders are not printed on the FTC pages. The September 2025 final order date is inferred from an article date. The outcome of the Media Matters appeal and of the BlackRock motion to dismiss were not found. Private equity enforcement relating to ESG was not found, though FTC private equity cases on other theories exist and were not assessed. Whether these ad-agency actions count as 'ESG/DEI collusion' is a classification judgment: the FTC frames them as viewpoint-based boycotts. Update 2026-10-15: the FTC's own releases for the April 2026 and June 2026 agency orders were located and replace the earlier law-firm, local-news and proskauer sourcing for those events (the Havas date is corrected from the 2026-07-05 news-report date to the 2026-06-30 FTC release). Searches found no FTC consent order, 6(b) study, policy statement or workshop on ESG or DEI coordination after July 2026, and no task force.
